label: Kimi K3.1 Pro
output:
**Four stars: a substantial improvement over our webcam, but not a cure-all**

**My rating is 4 out of 5 stars.** We bought the Lindqvist Optics PT-20 from Chancel AV in February 2026 for $2,140, plus $95 for the wall mount. It replaced the webcam we had been using to livestream worship since 2020. I’m a pastor, not an engineer, so this is my experience rather than a technical bench test.

Our nave is 92 feet long, and the camera is mounted on the balcony rail at the back. The 20x optical zoom is genuinely useful at that distance. We have nine presets stored: altar, pulpit, lectern, font, choir loft, piano, a wide view, and two positions for the chancel steps. The camera provides 1080p60 video, NDI HX, and a plain HDMI output. We run it into OBS on our old office PC and stream to YouTube, where we usually have 30–60 viewers on a Sunday.

PoE was important for us because it meant one cable up to the balcony rather than arranging separate power there. Day-to-day operation has been easier than I expected. Erik, our 16-year-old acolyte, controls the camera from the free web app on a tablet. He learned it in one afternoon and now handles it during worship.

The improvement in the picture was immediately worthwhile, especially for people watching from home. Delores, who is 82 and homebound, called to tell us she could finally read the hymn numbers on the board. That phone call told me more about whether the purchase was worthwhile than any specification sheet could.

Low-light performance is better, though not miraculous. At our Easter Vigil in April, during the candlelight portion and the first singing of “Christ the Lord Is Risen Today,” the picture became grainy with only the candles for light. It remained usable, however. Our old webcam would have shown little more than dots in those conditions. I would describe the PT-20 as significantly better in dim light, not as something that makes darkness disappear.

We did have two operational issues. On the first Sunday, the presets drifted a few degrees by the time we reached the sermon. That was frustrating, but the firmware 2.4 update in March fixed it. Autofocus also tends to hunt when someone walks between the camera and the pulpit. Our workaround is to lock the focus on the presets, which has worked well for us.

The manual is thin and badly translated, and it did not answer several basic questions well. On the other hand, Chancel AV’s phone support was excellent. Marcy was patient and clear, and she did not make me feel foolish for asking questions. That support mattered.

People should also understand what this camera does **not** do. Audio is not its job. It did nothing to fix our sound problem, and buying a better camera will not make an inadequate microphone or sound system suddenly work. We still have to address that separately.

Would I buy it again? Yes, and the four-star rating reflects both the real improvement and the frustrations with the initial preset drift, autofocus behavior, and manual. But $2,140, plus mounting and the rest of the streaming arrangement, is a considerable expense for a small church. If your room is shorter, your lighting is good, and your viewers mainly need a dependable wide view, a congregation under 100 might do perfectly well with something cheaper. For our long nave, multiple worship positions, and homebound members, the PT-20 has earned its place.
